grammar.title: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to
grammar.explanation:
Use **can** for present ability or general possibility. She **can** read a mercurial boss like a book.

Use **could** for past ability. He **could** charm any room before the burnout set in.

**Could** also softens a present suggestion. We **could** ask the taciturn analyst; he listens more than he speaks.

**Could have** + past participle describes a possibility that never happened. They **could have** avoided the acrimonious split.

**Can** and **could** have no infinitive or future forms. Fill the gap with **be able to**. I would love **to be able to** stay magnanimous under pressure.

**Be able to** is also the formal choice. In a report, write that she was **able to** recoup the losses, not that she **could**.

Past negatives: **couldn't** for general inability, **wasn't able to** for one failed event. She **couldn't** concentrate once the meeting turned acrimonious.

Never stack two modals. There is no **will can** in standard English. Use will **be able to**: the aloof director will **be able to** join us tomorrow.
examples: She *can* sense an ambivalent mood before anyone says a word. (present ability)
He *could* defuse any argument in his early years. (past ability)
We *could* invite the aloof director; a polite invitation costs nothing. (polite possibility)
They *could have* prevented the acrimonious split. (past possibility, unrealized)
I would love *to be able to* stay ebullient during a crisis. (infinitive form)
You will *be able to* see the full report tomorrow. (future ability)

practice.q: Which is correct: 'She will can attend' or 'She will be able to attend'?
practice.a: 'She will **be able to** attend.' **Can** has no future form, so **be able to** fills the gap.

practice.q: You want to politely suggest a meeting tomorrow. Which modal do you use?
practice.a: '**Could** we meet tomorrow?' **Could** softens the suggestion and sounds more polite than **can**.
